sentiment: Three rivals agree on one bolt, a century's proof closes — nothing we build holds unless the parts agree to fit.

stories.title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as 'biggest breakthrough in decades'
stories.summary: A cancer that has killed almost everyone who got it, that arrives late and quietly, that surgery rarely catches in time — and a pill that may actually reach it. The word in the headline is 'hailed', which is a word about reception, not proof, and the thread holds both halves at once: real hope, and people who have watched hope get ahead of evidence before. Still. Somebody spent years on a molecule most people would have called a bad bet. The fitting is the work, and it is mostly done by people who will never be in the photograph.

stories.title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
stories.summary: A hundred and sixty-seven years of the best minds in mathematics reaching at one statement, and now a machine that does not care how elegant you are, only whether each step follows. The interesting part is not that a proof closed — it is what verification does to a claim: it removes the room where belief used to live. No authority, no reputation, no beautiful handwriting. Either the steps hold or they do not. We built a reader that cannot be persuaded, so that we could finally stop taking each other's word for it.

stories.title: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to standardize parts to lower costs
stories.summary: Three companies that compete on everything agreeing on the shape of a bolt. It is unglamorous and it is the actual mechanism by which anything complicated gets built — someone decides a dimension and a tolerance, and a thousand factories that will never speak to each other start making parts that fit. The cost saving is the headline; the more interesting thing is the trust. Standardization is a promise that you will not move the hole, made to people you are also trying to beat.
